lines: A four-channel spectrum analyzer with the short-time Fourier transform laid out as controls: window, buffer length, hop rate, both axis scales, smoothing in time and frequency, and a display tilt.
Sets the gain on that input before analysis, from silence up to 12dB; the colour beside it is the colour of the curve it draws.
Stops and starts the buffering of fresh audio; switched off, the display holds the analysis it last made.
Chooses one of fifteen window functions applied to the buffer before the transform, which trades frequency resolution against spectral leakage.
Sets the size of the analysis buffer as a power of two, 128 samples up to 16384; a longer buffer resolves closer frequencies and costs more processing.
Sets how much time passes between one analysis and the next, 5ms to 300ms, which is also how often the display is redrawn.
Chooses whether the frequency axis is spaced linearly or logarithmically.
Chooses whether the level axis runs linearly from 0% to 400% of headroom, or in decibels from -60dB or -120dB up to 12dB.
Sets the time constant of the averaging applied across successive analyses, 0 to 2500ms; about 250ms suits music.
Sets how wide a band of neighbouring frequency bins is averaged together, from none up to 2.5 octaves; 1/6 octave suits a buffer of 1024 samples or more.
Sets the lowest frequency drawn, 0Hz up to half the sample rate.
Sets the highest frequency drawn, 0Hz up to half the sample rate.
Tilts the drawn spectrum about 1kHz, -9 to +9dB per octave, to offset the fall of high frequency energy in music; 4.5 or 3 is the usual choice.
One of four audio inputs; every channel of a polyphonic cable is summed into it, and 5V counts as full scale.
Note — The module has no outputs. Audio patched in is analysed and drawn, and nothing comes back out.
Note — The ten green words along the bottom of the display are the controls themselves: drag one up or down to change it.
Note — Randomize leaves every control alone, so it cannot scramble an analysis setting you are working with.
Note — The low and high frequency limits and their defaults are rebuilt from the sample rate, so changing the engine rate resets the high limit to the new Nyquist frequency.
Menu — Filled Display — fills the area under each curve rather than drawing it as a line
Menu — Bezier Curve — draws each curve as a smooth spline rather than straight segments between bins
Menu — AC-coupled — passes each input through a DC blocker before the analysis
SpectrumAnalyzer.notes: getVoltageSum() sums every channel of a polyphonic cable into one analysis lane, so the module reads polyphony but does not display it channel by channel. There are no outputs at all. The gain parameters run 0 to 3.981 with a display base of -10 and a multiplier of 20, which is how the tooltip reads -inf dB to 12dB. The ten parameters along the bottom of the display and the four input gains all have positions, so all fifteen controls can be clicked for help; index order matches panel order left to right. Every parameter has randomizeEnabled set false (src/SpectrumAnalyzer.cpp:183-184). The maker's manual is written against version 2.0.1 and matches this build's controls.

lines: A spectrogram: the same Fourier analysis drawn as a scrolling image, frequency up the screen and time across it, with level shown as colour.
Sets the gain on the input before analysis, from silence up to 12dB; it comes up at 6dB.
Stops and starts the buffering of fresh audio; switched off, the image stops scrolling.
Chooses one of fifteen window functions applied to the buffer before the transform, which trades frequency resolution against spectral leakage.
Chooses whether the frequency axis up the image is spaced linearly or logarithmically.
Sets the time constant of the averaging applied across successive analyses, 0 to 2500ms.
Sets how wide a band of neighbouring frequency bins is averaged together, from none up to 2.5 octaves.
Sets the lowest frequency drawn, 0Hz up to half the sample rate.
Sets the highest frequency drawn, 0Hz up to half the sample rate.
Tilts the drawn spectrum about 1kHz, -9 to +9dB per octave, to offset the fall of high frequency energy in music.
The audio to analyse; every channel of a polyphonic cable is summed into it, and 5V counts as full scale. The maker left this jack named TODO, which is what its tooltip reads.
Note — The module has no outputs. Audio patched in is analysed and drawn, and nothing comes back out.
Note — The transform is fixed at 2048 samples and the image holds 512 columns of history; neither is adjustable, unlike the analyzer in this plugin.
Note — The seven green words along the bottom of the display are the controls themselves: drag one up or down to change it.
Menu — AC-coupled — passes the input through a DC blocker before the analysis
Menu — Color Map: Viridis, Cividis, Magma, Plasma, Inferno, Bone, Gray — chooses the colours level is drawn in
Spectrogram.notes: The one input is configured as configInput(INPUT_SIGNAL, "TODO") at src/Spectrogram.cpp:110, so Rack's own tooltip for that jack reads TODO. The parameter the panel prints as Y SCALE is the frequency scale, FrequencyScale Linear or Logarithmic, named "Y Scale" because the spectrogram draws frequency up the image rather than across it; the analyzer in the same plugin uses the same enumeration for its X SCALE. The shipped manual for Spectre is the Fourier manual with the module name left as Fourier in its header, and it documents Length, Hop, X-Scale and a magnitude Y-Scale, none of which exist on this panel: the FFT length is fixed at 2048 and the history at 512 columns (src/Spectrogram.cpp:27-28), and the only Y Scale is the frequency one. There are no outputs. Index order matches panel order.
